leading_positions.synthesis: Six of eight members list B012 (optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye) as their single preferred prize part. Four of them (Johansson, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) moved to it in round 1 from lower or different opening ranks, and Mehlig and Johansson placed it above their own opening first choices (B057, B051). They share the reading that the magic-wavelength lattice is a clean, quantitatively understood idea, that roughly 1e-18 uncertainties have been reproduced across several laboratories, and that the two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist. They do not share a view of how much the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize reduce novelty, whether the Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and ion-clock contributions need to be reflected in the names or the wording, or whether timing should follow the redefinition of the second. Kroll's support carries an explicit lineage disclosure, and Kroll also records that his preference partly reflects a specialist's view.

Eriksson alone prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) as the lead, as a prediction-then-confirmation story with independent reproduction in many laboratories and a platform that has opened further moire phases. Eriksson names B012 as the first alternative and says the clock is the more secure choice if the committee wants settled understanding. Mehlig, Johansson and Lindroth explicitly describe B036 as a candidate for a later year, citing the unresolved pairing mechanism and the age of the experiment, but none of them lists it as a preferred part.

Danielsson alone prefers the IceCube discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos (Halzen, Karle, Spiering) as the lead. Danielsson rests the case on the robustness of the diffuse flux, consistency with KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD, and the link to the origin of cosmic rays, and names B012 and B039 as alternatives. The chair, who ranked IceCube first at the opening and now prefers B012, and Olsson, who ranked it seventh, both describe the credit among a large collaboration and the Baikal and AMANDA predecessors as unresolved. Danielsson accepts the same concern, and the chair's own file now treats the IceCube credit as something to settle for a later year.

areas_of_agreement: Every member's preferred configuration is a single-part prize with one ballot ID; no member proposes a two-part or split prize in round 1, and several note that the three-laureate limit rules out pairing B012 with a full three-name second part.

All seven members who proposed laureates for B012 name the same two, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye, and nobody argues for adding a third name to the Katori-Ye pair, although several flag priority questions.
Members who prefer different candidates agree on the science of B012: Eriksson, Danielsson and others call the attribution clean and the result mature, and Danielsson says he would not block it.

Members across the preferred candidates treat the opening vote count as a different thing from scientific merit; those who moved to B012 say they did so on the record and the attribution, not on the number of supporters.

B057 (topological insulators) is described by Mehlig, Johansson, Lindroth, Olsson, Kroll, Eriksson and Pearce as having a credit gap, because Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not in the Kane, Mele, Molenkamp trio; Mehlig, who ranked it first at the opening, now keeps it only as a first alternative.
Members who comment on the pairing mechanism in B036 agree it is still debated; they differ on whether that should delay a prize.
scientific_disputes: Discovery or tool: Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig note that B012 is a measurement technology, with the fundamental-physics payoffs (varying constants, dark matter, geodesy, redefinition of the second) still prospective. Kroll says he does not block it but would prefer results about nature; Danielsson says much the same. Supporters answer that the redshift over millimetres and the 1e-18 agreement between independent clocks are already established results.

Distinctness of B012 from earlier prizes: Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce all raise the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. Supporters say the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation is distinct; Mehlig and Olsson want the citation worded narrowly around the lattice architecture so it does not read as general metrology. Whether ion-clock groups feel excluded is not settled.

B036 versus B012: Eriksson argues that surprising, theory-confirmed new states of matter outweigh the age of the experiment; Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce, who comment, point to the unsettled superconducting mechanism, twist-angle disorder and the field being only seven to eight years old. Johansson and Pearce say they defer to condensed-matter colleagues.

B029: the diffuse flux is described as robust by Danielsson, Pearce and Kroll, but Olsson and Danielsson note that source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) remain few and that these would implicate different people from a diffuse-flux citation.

B051 (circuit QED): Johansson ranked it first and Kroll sixth; the dispute is whether recognition of superconducting circuits in 2025 makes a second award on the same platform unwise, and whether the discovery can be separated from the engineering platform.
attribution_disputes: B012: Lemonde (SYRTE, including the parallel magic-wavelength and Hg lattice proposals), Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Boyd and the ion-clock groups are named by several members as outside the pair. Mehlig, Kroll and Lindroth want the 2001 to 2005 priority record checked; Olsson and Kroll add that the 1e-18 and redshift results belong to Ye's group, and so support the realization half of the citation rather than Katori's proposal.

B029: three names for a collaboration of several hundred, and the position of Baikal and AMANDA pioneers relative to Spiering, are unresolved. Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson say they cannot defend Halzen, Karle and Spiering as the right three without evidence on who made the decisive contributions; Danielsson and Pearce acknowledge the point.

B057: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang; with four named contributors competing for three places, Mehlig, Olsson, Johansson and Lindroth each describe it as the least settled among the well-supported candidates.

B036: Cao, Fatemi and other first authors, and Dean and Young on hBN-encapsulated moire work, fall outside the credited trio; Eriksson, Mehlig and Johansson ask whether Bistritzer should be named alongside MacDonald and whether the experimental record has been checked.

B039: Pearce and Danielsson chose different trios from the same four names (Della Negra versus Jenni) at the opening, and Pearce says this shows how contestable the credit is; Danielsson's round-1 file does not argue the point further.
B005 (mentioned by Eriksson and Olsson): the theory share is disputed (Butler versus Mathon and Umerski), though neither member lists B005 as preferred.
maturity_disputes: Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second before awarding B012: Olsson, Mehlig and Pearce state that the criterion does not depend on a standards-body decision, while Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth list timing as an open uncertainty.

Whether B036 is too early: Eriksson, Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce disagree on whether eight years of independent reproduction is enough when the pairing mechanism is open; Eriksson would not oppose B036 in a later year.
Whether B029 should wait for more source associations beyond the diffuse flux; Pearce and Olsson raise this and Danielsson accepts that the astrophysical interpretation is incomplete.
Whether B051 should wait because superconducting circuits were recognised in 2025.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Kroll disclosed time in John Hall's laboratory during his PhD; Hall was Jun Ye's doctoral advisor. He reports no joint work or financial interest with Katori or Ye, and notes the lineage for the committee.
Olsson disclosed that she has been a Fellow of the University of Tokyo since 2025 and that Katori is affiliated there; no collaboration with him is shown in her profile.

Johansson disclosed that B051 (circuit QED), his opening first choice, lies in his own field and that he directs the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology; he raised recusal or deference on B051, and some caution on B010 as adjacent. He reports no connection to B012.
Kroll noted that his WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Johansson works, relevant to B051.
Olsson disclosed that B021 (aberration-corrected electron optics) is in her own field and that she should not drive that discussion.

Pearce (chair) disclosed mild proximity to B029 through Fermi-LAT's participation in the TXS 0506+056 follow-up and a field close to neutrino astronomy, with no personal tie to the credited names, and no conflict on B012.

Danielsson, Eriksson, Lindroth and Mehlig reported no specific conflicts; Lindroth and Mehlig noted membership of the same broad atomic-physics or Gothenburg community without collaboration with the credited names.
questions_for_round2: Can the committee state, in a draft citation for B012, what is distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and does wording around the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice with many-atom interrogation settle the overlap concern raised by six members?

What does the priority record from about 2001 to 2005 show for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clocks (Katori, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Ye), and is it sufficient for Katori and Ye to be the only two names, or does any member propose a change?

Should the 1e-18 accuracy, millimetre redshift and many-body results be attributed to Ye in the citation text, with Katori credited for the proposal and early demonstrations, as Olsson and Kroll suggest?

Is the expected redefinition of the second a legitimate consideration for timing, or should the committee decide on the demonstrated science alone, as Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce argue and Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth leave open?
Does Kroll's lineage through John Hall's laboratory, or Olsson's University of Tokyo fellowship, require any procedural step if B012 advances, and how should those disclosures be recorded?

For Eriksson, what specifically would make B036 ready this year, and can the committee verify the experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young) and the Bistritzer share well enough to name MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer?

For Danielsson, is there a citation for B029 that rests on the diffuse flux alone and a defensible trio from a collaboration of hundreds with Baikal and AMANDA predecessors, and what evidence would answer Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson on who made the decisive contributions?
Should B057 be revisited only if a fairer set of names including the HgTe prediction can be found within the three-person limit, and does the 2016 prize leave enough unclaimed ground?
summary.chair_observation: In round 1 the explicit preferred configurations are B012 (six members), B036 (Eriksson) and B029 (Danielsson), all single-part prizes. The two minority leads are each recorded by their proposers with the same attribution and maturity cautions that the B012 supporters apply to their own choice, and no member lists B057, B051, B010, B039 or any other candidate as a preferred part. This summary counts only positions stated in the eight round-1 files; the chair is also a B012 supporter and has tried to present the B036 and B029 cases in their proposers' own terms. Round 2 should focus on the B012 citation and priority questions and on whether Eriksson and Danielsson can accept it or want to press their own candidates.
